newsitem.title: PERU: Red Cross wins plaudits in Peru hostage crisis.
newsitem.headline: Red Cross wins plaudits in Peru hostage crisis.

text.p: Michel Minnig, the top Red Cross official in Peru, must have lost count of the number of times he has walked up to the elegant portals of the Japanese ambassador's home in Lima in the last 13 days.

Under the glare of the world's press, Minnig and his young team braved the guns of the heavily armed band of Marxist rebels, who stormed a lavish party at the residence on Dec. 17, to open lines of communication.

While the Peruvian government maintained a tough stance, refusing until Saturday even to meet the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) guerrillas, the Red Cross stepped into the void, acting as a go-between for the residence and the world outside.

It has been an enormous responsibility for the Geneva-based International Committee of the Red Cross and one which contrasts with its traditional low-key image of tending to victims of war and internal conflict.
"The Red Cross has come of age during this crisis, it has carved itself a new niche," said one western diplomat, who asked not to be named.
Minnig, however, rejects the idea that the Red Cross has adopted a new role in the Peruvian crisis.
"The rules of the International Committee of the Red Cross have not changed but its perception has changed through this crisis," he said in a television interview on Sunday.
Minnig, who has been in Peru less than three months, was at the ill-fated reception when the guerrillas burst in through a hole they had blown in the outer wall of the property.

When police were firing tear gas cannisters into the building in an effort to flush out the rebels Minnig shouted out to them to hold their fire. Shortly afterward he secured the release of all women and many of the elderly.
Minnig left with the first group of hostages but he did not walk away from the crisis.
"He (Minnig) has had an extraordinary role in all of this. We owe a lot to him," said Carlos Aquino Rodriguez, a university profesor released on Dec. 22.
The tall, blond Swiss has visited the building daily, speaking to rebels and hostages in the same earnest tones.
"He never stopped moving and talking. I never saw him standing still," Aquino said.
Minnig, with 10 years service for the Red Cross including stints in Nicaragua, Iraq, Sudan and Bosnia, said he was guided by a simple philosophy.
"I am generally concerned about people who find themselves in difficult situations," he said in the television interview.
In the early days of the siege, with hundreds of hostages still inside, the Red Cross struggled to meet their basic needs.
Former captives recount sharing a piece of bread between five and lining up to use one of the house's four bathrooms.
But as the crisis dragged on, the organisation called in reinforcements and organised a coordinated plan to improve conditions inside the home.

Hostages now receive two balanced meals per day and have been given fresh clothes, toothbrushes, messages from relatives and even boardgames. Fourteen field latrines were brought in to relieve pressure on the bathrooms, and lanterns and water were supplied to make up for mains supplies cut off early in the siege.
When the residence's generator ran out of fuel, throwing the home into complete darkness, Minnig again stepped up.
With rebels and hostages convinced that a military attack was imminent, Minnig spent the night inside.
"The fact that a Red Cross man was inside calmed things. His presence was a guarantee that the police wouldn't attack," Aquino said.
